modern: The streams of living water that flow from Jerusalem are no more dried up by the parching heat of sultry midsummer than they were frozen by the cold winds of blustering winter. Rejoice, my soul, that you have been kept alive to testify to the faithfulness of the Lord. The seasons change, and you change, but your Lord stays forever the same, and the streams of his love are as deep, as broad and as full as ever. The heat of business worries and scorching trials makes me need the cooling streams of the river of his grace; I can go at once and drink my fill from the inexhaustible fountain, for in summer and in winter it pours out its flood. The upper springs never run low, and, blessed be the name of the Lord, the lower springs can’t fail either. Elijah found the brook Cherith dry up, but Jehovah was still the same God of providence. Job said his brothers were like deceitful brooks, but he found his God an overflowing river of comfort. The Nile is Egypt’s great confidence, but its floods vary; our Lord is forever the same. Cyrus took the city of Babylon by turning the course of the Euphrates, but no power, human or hellish, can turn aside the current of divine grace. The beds of ancient rivers have been found all dry and desolate, but the streams that rise on the mountains of divine sovereignty and infinite love will always be full to the brim. Generations melt away, but the course of grace never changes. The river of God can sing with more truth than the brook in the poem—

How happy you are, my soul, to be led beside such still waters! Never wander off to other streams, or you will hear the Lord’s rebuke: “What hast thou to do in the way of Egypt to drink of the muddy river?”

modern:
My soul, now that the cool of the day has come, withdraw for a while and listen to the voice of your God. He is always ready to speak with you when you are prepared to hear. If there is any slowness to meet, it isn’t on his part but entirely on yours, for he stands at the door and knocks, and if his people will only open, he is glad to come in. But what state is my heart in, my Lord’s garden? Dare I hope that it is well trimmed and watered and bearing fruit fit for him? If not, he will have a great deal to rebuke; but still I ask him to come to me, for nothing can so surely bring my heart into the right condition as the presence of the Sun of Righteousness, who brings healing in his wings.

Come, then, O Lord my God; my soul earnestly invites you and eagerly waits for you. Come to me, O Jesus, my well-beloved, and plant fresh flowers in my garden, like those I see blooming so perfectly in your matchless character! Come, O my Father, who are the Gardener, and deal with me in your tenderness and wisdom! Come, O Holy Spirit, and water my whole nature with dew, as the plants are now moistened with the evening dew. Oh, that God would speak to me! Speak, Lord, for your servant is listening! Oh, that he would walk with me! I am ready to give up my whole heart and mind to him, and every other thought is hushed. I am only asking for what he delights to give. I am sure he will stoop to have fellowship with me, for he has given me his Holy Spirit to live with me forever. Sweet is the cool twilight, when every star seems like an eye of heaven, and the cool wind is like the breath of heavenly love. My Father, my elder Brother, my sweet Comforter, speak now in loving kindness, for you have opened my ear and I am not rebellious.

modern: It is a blessed fact that Christians can rejoice even in the deepest distress. Though trouble surrounds them, they still sing, and like many birds, they sing best in their cages. The waves may roll over them, but their souls soon rise to the surface and see the light of God’s face. They have a buoyancy that keeps their heads always above water and helps them sing in the middle of the storm, “God is with me still.” To whom should the glory go? Oh, to Jesus; it is all by Jesus. Trouble doesn’t necessarily bring comfort with it to the believer, but the presence of the Son of God in the fiery furnace with him fills his heart with joy. He is sick and suffering, but Jesus visits him and makes his bed for him. He is dying, and the cold, chilly waters of Jordan are rising around him up to his neck, but Jesus puts his arms around him and cries, “Don’t be afraid, my dear one. To die is to be blessed. The waters of death have their source in heaven. They aren’t bitter; they are as sweet as nectar, for they flow from the throne of God.” As the departing saint wades through the stream, and the waves gather around him, and heart and flesh fail him, the same voice sounds in his ears: “Fear not; I am with thee; be not dismayed; I am thy God.” As he nears the edge of the infinite unknown, and is almost too frightened to enter the land of the dead, Jesus says, “Fear not, it is your Father’s good pleasure to give you the kingdom.” Strengthened and comforted like this, the believer isn’t afraid to die. No, he is even willing to depart, for since he has seen Jesus as the morning star, he longs to gaze on him as the sun in its strength. Truly, the presence of Jesus is all the heaven we want. He is at once

modern: A cry is the natural expression of sorrow, and a fitting one when every other way of appealing fails us. But the cry must be directed to the Lord alone, for to cry to man is to waste our pleas on the air. When we consider how ready the Lord is to hear and how able he is to help, we will see good reason to direct all our appeals straight to the God of our salvation. It will be useless to call to the rocks on the day of judgment, but our Rock listens to our cries.

“*Be not silent to me*.” Mere formalists may be content without answers to their prayers, but genuine petitioners can’t be. They aren’t satisfied with what prayer does by itself in calming the mind and quieting the will. They must go further and get actual replies from heaven, or they can’t rest; and they long to receive those replies at once, for they dread even a little of God’s silence. God’s voice is often so terrible that it shakes the wilderness; but his silence is just as full of awe to an eager petitioner. When God seems to close his ear, we mustn’t close our mouths for that reason, but cry more earnestly still; for when our note grows shrill with eagerness and grief, he won’t refuse us a hearing for long. What a dreadful condition we would be in if the Lord were to become silent to our prayers forever! “*Lest, if thou be silent to me, I become like them that go down into the pit*.” Deprived of the God who answers prayer, we would be in a more pitiable plight than the dead in the grave, and would soon sink to the same level as the lost in hell. We *must* have answers to prayer. Ours is an urgent case of desperate need. Surely the Lord will speak peace to our troubled minds, for he can never find it in his heart to let his own chosen ones perish.

modern:
Pharaoh’s dream has too often been my waking experience. My days of laziness have ruinously destroyed everything I gained in times of eager work. My seasons of coldness have frozen all the warm glow of my times of fervor and enthusiasm. And my fits of worldliness have thrown me back from my progress in the divine life. I need to beware of lean prayers, lean praises, lean duties and lean experiences, for these will eat up the fat of my comfort and peace. If I neglect prayer for even the shortest time, I lose all the spirituality I had reached. If I draw no fresh supplies from heaven, the old grain in my granary is soon eaten up by the famine raging in my soul. When the caterpillars of indifference, the cankerworms of worldliness and the palmerworms of self-indulgence lay my heart completely waste and make my soul wither, all my former fruitfulness and growth in grace does me no good at all.

How eager I should be to have no lean days, no ugly hours! If every day I traveled toward the goal of my desires, I would soon reach it; but backsliding leaves me still far from the prize of my high calling, and robs me of the progress I had made so laboriously. The only way all my days can be like the “fat kine” is to feed them in the right meadow: to spend them with the Lord, in his service, in his company, in his fear and in his way. Why shouldn’t every year be richer than the last in love and usefulness and joy? I am nearer the heavenly hills; I have had more experience of my Lord, and I should be more like him. O Lord, keep the curse of leanness of soul far from me. Don’t let me have to cry, “My leanness, my leanness, woe unto me!” but may I be well fed and nourished in your house, so that I may praise your name.

modern:
We *mustn’t imagine that we are suffering for Christ, and with Christ, if we aren’t in Christ*. Dear friend, are you trusting in Jesus alone? If not, whatever you may have to mourn over on earth, you aren’t “suffering with Christ,” and have no hope of reigning with him in heaven. Nor should we conclude that all a Christian’s sufferings are sufferings with Christ, for *he must be called by God to suffer*. If we are rash and reckless, and rush into situations that neither providence nor grace has fitted us for, we should ask ourselves whether we aren’t sinning rather than sharing fellowship with Jesus. If we let passion take the place of judgment, and self-will rule instead of the authority of Scripture, we will fight the Lord’s battles with the devil’s weapons, and if we cut our own fingers we mustn’t be surprised.

Again, *when troubles come on us as the result of sin, we mustn’t dream that we are suffering with Christ*. When Miriam spoke against Moses and leprosy struck her, she wasn’t suffering for God. Moreover, suffering that God accepts *must have God’s glory as its aim*. If I suffer to make a name for myself or win applause, I will get no reward but the Pharisee’s. It is also necessary *that love for Jesus and love for his chosen people always be the mainspring of all our patience. We must show the Spirit of Christ* in meekness, gentleness and forgiveness. Let’s search and see whether we truly *suffer with Jesus*.

And if we do suffer with him like this, what is our “light affliction” compared with *reigning with him*? Oh, it is so blessed to be in the furnace with Christ, and such an honor to stand in the pillory with him, that even if there were no future reward we might count ourselves happy in the honor we have now. But when the reward is so eternal, so infinitely more than we had any right to expect, won’t we take up the cross eagerly and go on our way rejoicing?

modern:
Sanctification begins in regeneration. The Spirit of God puts into a person the new living principle by which he becomes “a new creature” in Christ Jesus. This work, which begins in the new birth, is carried on in two ways. One is mortification, by which the lusts of the flesh are put down and kept under. The other is vivification, by which the life God has put within us is made a well of water springing up to everlasting life. This is carried on every day in what is called “perseverance,” by which the Christian is kept and continued in a state of grace and made to abound in good works, to the praise and glory of God. And it reaches its height, its perfection, in “glory,” when the soul, thoroughly cleansed, is caught up to live with holy beings at the right hand of the Majesty on high.

But while the Spirit of God is the author of sanctification, there is also a visible means he uses, and it mustn’t be forgotten. “Sanctify them,” said Jesus, “through thy *truth*: thy word is truth.” There are very many passages of Scripture that prove the Word of God is the instrument of our sanctification. The Spirit of God brings the commands and teachings of the truth to our minds and applies them with power. These are heard with the ear, and when they are received into the heart, they work in us both to will and to do God’s good pleasure. The truth is what makes us holy, and if we don’t hear or read the truth, we won’t grow in holiness. We only make progress in sound living as we make progress in sound understanding. “Thy word is a lamp unto my feet and a light unto my path.” Don’t say of any error, “It is a mere matter of opinion.” No one indulges an error of judgment without sooner or later tolerating an error in practice. Hold fast to the truth, for by holding to it you will be made holy by the Spirit of God.

modern: Outward, practical holiness is a very precious mark of grace. It is to be feared that many who profess the faith have twisted the doctrine of justification by faith in such a way as to treat good works with contempt. If so, they will receive everlasting contempt on the last great day. If our hands aren’t clean, let’s wash them in Jesus’ precious blood, and so lift up pure hands to God. But “*clean hands*” won’t be enough unless they go with “*a pure heart*.” True religion is heart-work. We may wash the outside of the cup and the plate as long as we like, but if the inside is filthy, we are filthy altogether in the sight of God, for our hearts are more truly ourselves than our hands are. The very life of our being lies in our inner nature, and that is why purity within is so urgently needed. The pure in heart will see God; everyone else is just a blind bat.

The man who is born for heaven “*hath not lifted up his soul unto vanity*.” Everyone has joys that lift up their souls. The worldly man lifts up his soul in fleshly pleasures, which are mere empty vanities; but the saint loves more solid things. Like Jehoshaphat, he is lifted up in the ways of the Lord. Whoever is content with pig food will be counted with the pigs. Does the world satisfy you? Then you have your reward and your portion in this life. Make the most of it, for you will know no other joy.

“*Nor sworn deceitfully*.” The saints are still people of honor. A Christian’s word is his only oath, but it is as good as twenty oaths from other people. False speaking will shut anyone out of heaven, for a liar won’t enter God’s house, whatever he may claim or do. Reader, does the text in front of you condemn you, or do you hope to go up into the hill of the Lord?

modern:
We are very inclined to think of the saints of the apostles’ time as if they were “saints” in some more special way than the rest of God’s children. All whom God has called by his grace and made holy by his Spirit are “saints”; but we tend to look on the *apostles* as extraordinary beings, hardly subject to the same weaknesses and temptations as we are. Yet in doing so we forget this truth: the closer a man lives to God, the more intensely he has to mourn over his own evil heart; and the more his Master honors him in his service, the more the evil of the flesh troubles and torments him day after day. The fact is, if we had seen the apostle Paul, we would have thought him remarkably like the rest of the chosen family. And if we had talked with him, we would have said, “We find that his experience and ours are much the same. He is more faithful, more holy and more deeply taught than we are, but he has the very same trials to endure. In fact, in some ways he is tried more severely than we are.”

So don’t look on the saints of old as free from weaknesses or sins, and don’t regard them with that mystical reverence that would almost make us idol-worshipers. Their holiness is within reach even for us. We are “called to be saints” by the same voice that drew them to their high calling. It is a Christian’s duty to press his way into the inner circle of saintliness; and if these saints were ahead of us in what they reached, as they certainly were, let’s follow them. Let’s imitate their zeal and holiness. We have the same light they had; the same grace is open to us; so why should we be satisfied until we have equaled them in heavenly character? They lived *with* Jesus, they lived *for* Jesus, and so they grew *like* Jesus. Let’s live by the same Spirit they did, “looking unto Jesus,” and our saintliness will soon be plain to see.

modern:
Since we have such a God to trust, let’s rest on him with all our weight. Let’s resolutely drive out all unbelief and try to get rid of the doubts and fears that so spoil our comfort, since there is no excuse for fear where God is the foundation of our trust. A loving parent would be deeply hurt if his child couldn’t trust him; and how ungenerous, how unkind our behavior is when we put so little confidence in our heavenly Father, who has never failed us and never will! It would be good if doubting were banished from God’s household; but it is to be feared that old Unbelief is as nimble these days as when the psalmist asked, “Is his mercy clean gone for ever? Will he be favourable no more?”

David hadn’t given the mighty sword of the giant Goliath a very long trial, and yet he said, “There is none like it.” He had tried it once, in the hour of his youthful victory, and it had proved to be made of the right metal, and so he praised it ever afterward. In the same way we should speak well of our God; there is none like him in heaven above or on the earth beneath. “To whom then will ye liken me, or shall I be equal? saith the Holy One.” There is no rock like the Rock of Jacob, as even our enemies admit. Far from letting doubts live in our hearts, we will take the whole hateful crew, as Elijah did the prophets of Baal, and kill them at the brook; and for a stream to kill them at, we will choose the sacred torrent that pours from our Savior’s wounded side. We have been through many trials, but we have never yet been thrown anywhere where we couldn’t find in our God everything we needed. So let’s be encouraged to trust in the Lord forever, sure that his everlasting strength will be, as it has been, our help and support.

modern:
Divine love stands out most when it shines in the middle of judgments. Fair is that lone star that smiles through the gaps in the thunderclouds; bright is the oasis that blooms in the wilderness of sand; just as fair and bright is love in the middle of wrath. When the Israelites provoked the Most High by their constant idolatry, he punished them by holding back both dew and rain, so that a severe famine came on their land. But while he did this, he made sure his own chosen ones were safe. If every other brook is dry, there will still be one kept for Elijah; and when that fails, God will still keep a place of food for him. And not only that: the Lord didn’t have just one “Elijah.” He had a remnant according to the election of grace, hidden by fifties in a cave; and though the whole land was in the grip of famine, these fifties in the cave were fed, and fed from Ahab’s own table too, by his faithful, God-fearing steward Obadiah.

Let’s draw this conclusion from it: come what may, God’s people are safe. Let earthquakes shake the solid earth; let the skies themselves be torn in two; yet in the wreck of worlds the believer will be as secure as in the calmest hour of rest. If God can’t save his people *under* heaven, he will save them *in* heaven. If the world becomes too hot to hold them, then heaven will be the place where they are received and kept safe. So be confident when you hear of wars and rumors of wars. Don’t let any upheaval distress you, but be quiet from fear of evil. Whatever comes on the earth, you will be secure beneath Jehovah’s broad wings. Lean on his promise; rest in his faithfulness; and defy the blackest future, for there is nothing dreadful in it for you. Your only concern should be to show the world how blessed it is to listen to the voice of wisdom.

modern:
Have you ever really weighed and thought about how great the sin of God’s people is? Think how hateful your own wrongdoing is, and you will find that it isn’t just a sin here and there towering up like an Alp, but that your sins are heaped on one another, as in the old legend of the giants who piled Pelion on Ossa, mountain on mountain. What a total of sin there is in the life of even one of the holiest of God’s children! Try multiplying this, the sin of just one, by the whole multitude of the redeemed, “a number which no man can number,” and you will have some idea of the great mass of guilt of the people for whom Jesus shed his blood.

But we get a better idea of how great sin is from the greatness of the remedy provided. It is the blood of Jesus Christ, God’s only and dearly loved Son. God’s Son! Angels throw their crowns down before him! All the choirs of heaven surround his glorious throne. “God over all, blessed for ever. Amen.” And yet he takes on himself the form of a servant, and is whipped and pierced, bruised and torn, and at last killed; since nothing but the blood of the Son of God in human flesh could make atonement for our offenses. No human mind can properly measure the infinite value of the divine sacrifice, for great as the sin of God’s people is, the atonement that takes it away is immeasurably greater.

So the believer, even when sin rolls over him like a black flood and the memory of the past is bitter, can still stand before the blazing throne of the great and holy God and cry, “Who is he that condemneth? It is Christ that died; yea rather, that hath risen again.” While the memory of his sin fills him with shame and sorrow, he also uses it as a dark background to show off the brightness of mercy. Guilt is the dark night in which the fair star of God’s love shines with calm splendor.

modern: This one morning of the year we have kept to remind the reader about praying for ministers, and we most earnestly beg every Christian household to grant the urgent request of the text, first made by an apostle and now repeated by us. Brothers and sisters, our work is solemn and momentous, meaning well-being or ruin for thousands. We deal with souls for God on eternal business, and our word is either a fragrance of life leading to life, or of death leading to death. A very heavy responsibility rests on us, and it will be no small mercy if in the end we are found clear of the blood of all men. As officers in Christ’s army, we are the special target of the hatred of men and devils. They watch for us to stumble, and work hard to trip us up. Our sacred calling exposes us to temptations you are free from; above all, it too often draws us away from enjoying the truth for ourselves into thinking about it as ministers, in the line of duty. We meet many knotty cases, and our wits are at a loss. We see very sad backslidings, and our hearts are wounded. We see millions perishing, and our spirits sink. You don’t look to us but to our Master for spiritual blessings; and yet how many times he has given those blessings through his ministers! modern:
Saved one, think gratefully about this command of mercy. Notice that this decree of God is *majestic*. In our text we see a sinner with nothing in him but sin, expecting nothing but wrath; but the eternal Lord passes by in his glory. He looks, he pauses, and he speaks the single but royal word, “Live.” There speaks a God. Who but he could deal with life like this and hand it out with a single word?

Again, this decree is *many-sided*. When he says “Live,” it includes many things. Here is life in the eyes of the law: the sinner is about to be condemned, but the mighty One says, “Live,” and he rises pardoned and acquitted. It is spiritual life: we didn’t know Jesus; our eyes couldn’t see Christ, our ears couldn’t hear his voice; Jehovah said “Live,” and we who were dead in trespasses and sins were made alive. Moreover, it includes the life of glory, which is the perfection of spiritual life. “I said unto thee, Live”: and that word rolls on through all the years of time until death comes, and in the middle of the shadows of death the Lord’s voice is still heard: “Live!” On the morning of the resurrection it is that very same voice that the archangel echoes, “Live”; and as holy spirits rise to heaven to be blessed forever in the glory of their God, it is in the power of this same word, “Live.”

Notice again that it is an *irresistible* command. Saul of Tarsus is on the road to Damascus to arrest the saints of the living God. A voice is heard from heaven, and a light is seen brighter than the sun, and Saul is crying out, “Lord, what wilt thou have me to do?” This command is a command of *free grace*. When sinners are saved, it is only and entirely because God *will* do it, to magnify his free, unbought, unsought grace. Christians, see where you stand: debtors to grace. Show your gratitude by earnest, Christlike lives, and since God has told you to live, make sure you live in earnest.

modern:
Where does the secret strength of faith lie? It lies in the food it feeds on. Faith studies what the promise is: an outflowing of divine grace, an overflowing of the great heart of God. And faith says, “My God couldn’t have given this promise except out of love and grace, so it is quite certain his Word will be kept.” Then faith thinks, “*Who gave* this promise?” It considers not so much the promise’s greatness as the question, “Who is the author of it?” She remembers that it is God who cannot lie: God almighty, God unchanging. And so she concludes that the promise must be kept, and she presses forward in this firm conviction. She remembers *why the promise was given*: for God’s glory. And she feels perfectly sure that God’s glory is safe, that he will never stain his own coat of arms or dim the luster of his own crown; and so the promise must and will stand.

Then faith also considers the amazing *work of Christ* as clear proof that the Father means to keep his word. “He that spared not his own Son, but freely delivered him up for us all, how shall he not with him also freely give us all things?” Moreover, faith looks back on *the past*, for her battles have strengthened her and her victories have given her courage. She remembers that God has never failed her; no, that he has never once failed any of his children. She remembers times of great danger when deliverance came, hours of terrible need when her strength matched her day; and she cries, “No, I will never be led to think that he can change and leave his servant now. Until now the Lord has helped me, and he will help me still.” So faith sees each promise in its connection with the one who gave it, and because she does, she can say with assurance, “Surely goodness and mercy shall follow me all the days of my life!”

modern:
When the believer has begun to walk in the way of the Lord with trembling feet, he asks to be led onward still, like a little child held up by its parent’s helping hand, and he longs to be taught more of the alphabet of truth. Teaching by experience is the heart of this prayer. David knew a great deal, but he felt his ignorance and wanted to stay in the Lord’s school: four times over in two verses he applies for a scholarship in the college of grace. It would be good for many who profess the faith if, instead of following their own ideas and cutting out new paths of thought for themselves, they would ask for the good old ways of God’s own truth, and beg the Holy Spirit to give them holy understandings and teachable spirits.

“*For thou art the God of my salvation*.” Jehovah, three in one, is the Author and Perfecter of his people’s salvation. Reader, is he the God of *your* salvation? Do you find in the Father’s choosing, in the Son’s atonement and in the Spirit’s life-giving work all the grounds of your eternal hopes? If so, you can use this as an argument for getting further blessings: if the Lord has decided to save you, surely he won’t refuse to teach you his ways. It is a happy thing when we can speak to the Lord with the confidence David shows here; it gives us great power in prayer and comfort in trouble.

“*On thee do I wait all the day*.” Patience is the fair servant and daughter of faith; we wait cheerfully when we are sure we won’t wait in vain. It is our duty and our privilege to wait on the Lord all the days of our life, in service, in worship, in expectation and in trust. Our faith will be tested faith, and if it is the real thing, it will bear continued testing without giving way. We won’t grow tired of waiting on God if we remember how long and how graciously he once waited for us.

modern:
It is a delightful and profitable thing to trace the hand of God in the lives of the saints of old, and to see his goodness in rescuing them, his mercy in pardoning them and his faithfulness in keeping his covenant with them. But wouldn’t it be even more interesting and profitable for us to notice the hand of God in our own lives? Shouldn’t we look on our own history as at least as full of God, as full of his goodness and his truth, as much a proof of his faithfulness and truthfulness, as the lives of any of the saints who have gone before? We do our Lord an injustice when we suppose that he did all his mighty acts and showed himself strong for people in the early days, but doesn’t work wonders or bare his arm for the saints now on the earth.

Let’s review our own lives. Surely in them we can find some happy incidents, refreshing to ourselves and glorifying to our God. Have you had no *deliverances*? Have you passed through no rivers, held up by the divine presence? Have you walked through no fires unharmed? Have you had no *times when God showed himself to you*? Have you had no *choice favors*? The God who gave Solomon the desire of his heart, has he never listened to you and answered your requests? That God of lavish generosity of whom David sang, “Who satisfieth thy mouth with good things,” has he never filled *you* with good things? Have you never been made to lie down in green pastures? Have you never been led by the still waters? Surely the goodness of God has been the same to us as to the saints of old. So let’s weave his mercies into a song. Let’s take the pure gold of thankfulness and the jewels of praise and make them into another crown for the head of Jesus. Let our souls give out music as sweet and stirring as ever came from David’s harp, while we praise the Lord whose mercy endures forever.

modern:
A believer has two principles at work within him. In his natural state he was under one principle only, and that was darkness. Now light has come in, and the two principles are at odds. Notice the apostle Paul’s words in the seventh chapter of Romans: “I find then a law, that, when I would do good, evil is present with me. For I delight in the law of God after the inward man: but I see another law in my members, warring against the law of my mind, and bringing me into captivity to the law of sin, which is in my members.” How does this state of things come about? “The Lord divided the light from the darkness.” Darkness by itself is quiet and undisturbed, but when the Lord sends light in, there is a conflict, for the one is opposed to the other: a conflict that will never stop until the believer is altogether light in the Lord.

If there is a division *within* the individual Christian, there is sure to be *a division outside* him. As soon as the Lord gives anyone light, he begins to separate himself from the darkness around him. He breaks away from a merely worldly religion of outward ceremony, for nothing less than the gospel of Christ will satisfy him now. He withdraws from worldly society and frivolous amusements and looks for the company of the saints, for “We know we have passed from death unto life, because we love the brethren.” The light gathers to itself, and the darkness to itself. What God has divided, let’s never try to unite. As Christ went outside the camp, bearing his disgrace, so let’s come out from the ungodly and be a people set apart for him. He was holy, harmless, undefiled, separate from sinners; and as he was, so we are to be nonconformists to the world, dissenting from all sin, and marked out from the rest of mankind by our likeness to our Master.

modern:
What does it mean that we are citizens of heaven? It means that *we are under heaven’s government*. Christ, the King of heaven, reigns in our hearts; our daily prayer is, “Thy will be done on earth as it is in heaven.” We gladly receive the proclamations issued from the throne of glory, and we cheerfully obey the decrees of the Great King.

Then, as citizens of the New Jerusalem, *we share heaven’s honors*. The glory that belongs to the blessed saints in heaven belongs to us, for we are already sons of God, already princes of the royal blood. Already we wear the spotless robe of Jesus’ righteousness; already we have angels for our servants, saints for our companions, Christ for our Brother, God for our Father, and a crown of immortality for our reward. We share the honors of citizenship, for we have come to the general assembly and church of the firstborn, whose names are written in heaven.

As citizens, we have *a shared right to all the property of heaven*. Ours are its gates of pearl and walls of chrysolite; ours the sky-blue light of the city that needs no candle and no light of the sun; ours the river of the water of life, and the twelve kinds of fruit that grow on the trees planted on its banks. There is nothing in heaven that doesn’t belong to us. “Things present, or things to come,” all are ours.

Also, as citizens of heaven we *enjoy its delights*. Do they rejoice there over sinners who repent, prodigals who have come home? So do we. Do they sing the glories of triumphant grace? We do the same. Do they throw their crowns at Jesus’ feet? Whatever honors we have, we throw there too. Are they charmed by his smile? It is no less sweet to us who live below. Do they look forward, waiting for his second coming? We too watch and long for his appearing. If, then, we are *citizens of heaven* like this, let our walk and our actions fit our high rank.

modern:
The evening was “darkness” and the morning was “light,” and yet *the two together are called by the name given to the light alone*! This is rather remarkable, but it matches spiritual experience exactly. In every believer there is darkness and light, and yet he isn’t to be called a sinner because there is sin in him, but a saint because he has some degree of holiness. This will be a most comforting thought to those who are mourning their weaknesses and asking, “Can I be a child of God while there is so much darkness in me?” Yes; for you, like the day, take your name not from the evening but from the morning; and the word of God speaks of you as if you were already as perfectly holy as you soon will be. You are called a child of light, though there is darkness in you still. You are named after the quality that is uppermost in God’s sight, the one that will one day be the only principle left.

Notice that *the evening comes first*. By nature we are darkness first in order of time, and the gloom often comes first in our sorrowful awareness, driving us to cry out in deep humiliation, “God be merciful to me, a sinner.” The morning has second place; it dawns when grace overcomes nature. It is a blessed saying of John Bunyan’s: “That which is last, lasts for ever.” What comes first gives way in due time to what comes last; but nothing comes after the last. So though you are darkness by nature, once you have become light in the Lord there is no evening to follow: “thy sun shall no more go down.” The first day, in this life, is an evening and a morning; but the second day, when we will be with God forever, will be a day with no evening, but one sacred, high, eternal noon.

modern:
You have seen the arch of heaven spanning the plain: its colors are glorious and its shades rare. It is beautiful, but sadly it passes away, and look, it is gone. The fair colors give way to fleecy clouds, and the sky is no longer bright with the tints of heaven. It isn’t *established*. How could it be? A glorious show made up of passing sunbeams and falling raindrops, how could it last? The graces of the Christian character mustn’t be like the rainbow in its passing beauty; on the contrary, they must be established, settled, lasting. Believer, try to make every good thing you have a lasting thing. May your character not be writing in the sand, but an inscription cut in rock! May your faith be no “baseless fabric of a vision,” but may it be built of material able to stand that terrible fire that will burn up the wood, hay and stubble of the hypocrite. May you be rooted and grounded in love. May your convictions be deep, your love real, your desires earnest. May your whole life be so settled and established that all the blasts of hell and all the storms of earth will never be able to move you.

But notice how this blessing of being “stablished in the faith” is won. The apostle’s words point us to *suffering* as the means God uses: “*After that ye have suffered awhile*.” It is no use hoping we will be well rooted if no rough winds pass over us. Those old knots on the root of the oak tree and those strange twists in its branches all tell of the many storms that have swept over it, and they also show how deep its roots have forced their way. In the same way the Christian is made strong and firmly rooted by all the trials and storms of life. So don’t shrink from the stormy winds of trial, but take comfort, believing that by their rough discipline God is fulfilling this blessing for you.

modern:
In this simple way, by God’s grace, a living witness for the truth is always to be kept alive in the land: the Lord’s dear people are to hand down their testimony to the gospel and the covenant to their heirs, and these again to the next generation. This is our *first* duty. We are to begin at the family hearth; he is a bad preacher who doesn’t begin his ministry at home. The heathen are to be sought by every means, and the highways and hedges are to be searched, but home has the first claim, and woe to those who turn the Lord’s order upside down.

To teach our children is a *personal* duty. We can’t hand it over to Sunday school teachers or other friendly helpers. They can assist us, but they can’t release us from the sacred obligation. Proxies and sponsors are wicked inventions in this case. Mothers and fathers must, like Abraham, command their households in the fear of God, and talk with their children about the wonderful works of the Most High. Parents’ teaching is a *natural* duty: who is so fit to care for a child’s well-being as those who gave him his being? To neglect to teach our children is worse than the beasts. Family religion is *necessary* for the nation, for the family itself, and for the church of God. Roman Catholicism is quietly advancing in our land by a thousand schemes, and one of the most effective ways of resisting its advance is left almost neglected: teaching children the faith. *“Sanctified in Christ Jesus.”*

[[1Cor.1.2|1 Corinthians 1:2]]

*“Through sanctification of the Spirit.”*

[[1Pet.1.2|1 Peter 1:2]]

Notice how the three divine Persons act together in all their gracious acts. How unwisely those believers talk who prefer one Person of the Trinity to another; who think of Jesus as the embodiment of everything lovely and gracious, while they see the Father as severely just but without kindness. Those who exalt the Father’s decree and the Son’s atonement so as to belittle the work of the Spirit are just as wrong. In deeds of grace, none of the Persons of the Trinity acts apart from the others. They are as united in their deeds as in their being. In their love for the chosen they are one, and in the actions that flow from that great central source they are still undivided.

Notice this especially in the matter of sanctification. While we may rightly speak of sanctification as the work of the Spirit, we must take care not to see it as if the Father and the Son had no part in it. It is correct to speak of sanctification as the work of the Father, of the Son and of the Spirit. Jehovah still says, “Let *us* make man in our own image after our likeness,” and so we are “*his* workmanship, created in Christ Jesus unto good works, which God hath before ordained that we should walk in them.” See the value God puts on real holiness, since the three Persons of the Trinity are pictured working together to produce a church without “spot, or wrinkle, or any such thing.” And you, believer, as a follower of Christ, must also value holiness highly: purity of life and godliness of conduct. Value the blood of Christ as the foundation of your hope, but never speak slightingly of the work of the Spirit, which makes you fit for the inheritance of the saints in light. Today let’s live so as to show the work of the three-in-one God in us.

We will hold high conversation with the noble company of the chosen, all reigning with him who by his love and his mighty arm has brought them safely home. Heaven is a place of *victory made real*. Whenever, Christian, you have won a victory over your lusts—whenever, after hard struggling, you have laid a temptation dead at your feet—you have in that hour a foretaste of the joy that awaits you when the Lord will soon crush Satan under your feet and you will find yourself more than a conqueror through him who has loved you. modern:
Anger isn’t always or necessarily sinful, but it tends so strongly to run wild that whenever it shows itself we should be quick to question its character with this inquiry: “Doest thou well to be angry?” It may be that we can answer, “YES.” Very often anger is the madman’s firebrand, but sometimes it is Elijah’s fire from heaven. We do well when we are angry with sin because of the wrong it does against our good and gracious God; or with ourselves because we are still so foolish after so much divine teaching; or with others when the only cause of our anger is the evil they do. Whoever isn’t angry at wrongdoing becomes a sharer in it. Sin is a loathsome and hateful thing, and no renewed heart can patiently put up with it. God himself is angry with the wicked every day, and it is written in his Word, “Ye that love the Lord, hate evil.”

Far more often, it is to be feared, our anger isn’t praiseworthy or even justifiable, and then we must answer, “NO.” Why should we be irritable with children, hot-tempered with servants and furious with our companions? Is such anger a credit to our Christian profession, or does it glorify God? Isn’t it the old evil heart trying to regain control, and shouldn’t we resist it with all the strength of our newborn nature? Many who profess the faith give way to temper as if it were useless to try to resist; but let the believer remember that he must be a conqueror at every point, or he can’t be crowned. If we can’t control our tempers, what has grace done for us? Someone told Mr. Jay that grace was often grafted on a crab-stump. “Yes,” he said, “but the fruit will not be crabs.” We mustn’t make natural weakness an excuse for sin. We must run to the cross and pray the Lord to crucify our tempers and renew us in gentleness and meekness after his own image.

No human speech can express the full meaning of this delightful phrase, “*God is for me*.” He was “for us” before the worlds were made. He was “for us,” or he wouldn’t have given his dearly loved Son. He was “for us” when he struck his only Son and laid the full weight of his wrath on him; he was “for *us*,” though he was against *him*. He was “for us” when we were ruined in the fall; he loved us in spite of everything. He was “for us” when we were rebels against him, openly defying him. He was “for us,” or he wouldn’t have brought us humbly to seek his face. He has been “for us” in many struggles. We have been called to face whole armies of dangers; we have been attacked by temptations from outside and from within. How could we have stayed unharmed to this hour if he hadn’t been “for us”? He is “for us” with all the infinity of his being, with all the almighty power of his love, with all the unfailing wisdom of his mind. Clothed in all his divine attributes, he is “for us,” eternally and unchangeably “for us”: “for us” when those blue skies are rolled up like a worn-out garment; “for us” throughout eternity.

And because he is “for us,” the voice of prayer will always secure his help. “*When I cry unto thee, then shall mine enemies be turned back*.” This is no uncertain hope, but a well-grounded assurance: “*this I know*.” I will direct my prayer to you, and look up for the answer, sure that it will come and that my enemies will be defeated, “for God is for me.” O believer, how happy you are with the King of kings on your side! How safe, with such a Protector! How sure your cause, pleaded by such an Advocate! If God is for you, who can be against you?

modern: God’s altar was to be built of uncut stones, so that no trace of human skill or labor could be seen on it. Human wisdom loves to trim and arrange the teachings of the cross into a system more artificial and more to the taste of our corrupt fallen nature. But instead of improving the gospel, fleshly wisdom pollutes it, until it becomes another gospel and not the truth of God at all. Every alteration and amendment of the Lord’s own Word defiles and pollutes it. Man’s proud heart is very eager to have a hand in its own justification before God. People dream of preparations for Christ; they trust in humblings and repentings; they praise good works loudly; they boast greatly of natural ability; and in every way they try to lift human tools on the divine altar. It would be good if sinners would remember that, far from perfecting the Savior’s work, their fleshly confidences only pollute and dishonor it. The Lord alone must be exalted in the work of atonement, and not a single mark of man’s chisel or hammer will be tolerated. There is a built-in blasphemy in trying to add to what Christ Jesus, in his dying moments, declared finished, or to improve on what the Lord Jehovah finds perfectly satisfying. Trembling sinner, away with your tools! Fall on your knees in humble prayer; accept the Lord Jesus as the altar of your atonement, and rest in him alone.

Many who profess the faith may take warning from this morning’s text as to the doctrines they believe. There is far too much inclination among Christians to trim the truths of revelation square and make them fit neatly together. This is a form of irreverence and unbelief; let’s fight against it and receive the truth as we find it, rejoicing that the doctrines of the Word are uncut stones, and all the more fit for building an altar to the Lord.

modern:
Let’s learn from Mary Magdalene how to have fellowship with the Lord Jesus. Notice how she looked for him. She looked for the Savior *very early* in the morning. If you can wait for Christ, and are content to hope for fellowship with him at some distant time, you will never have fellowship at all; for the heart that is ready for fellowship is a hungering and thirsting heart. She also looked for him with *very great boldness*. Other disciples fled from the tomb, for they trembled and were amazed; but Mary, we are told, “stood” at the tomb. If you want Christ with you, look for him boldly. Let nothing hold you back. Defy the world. Press on where others run away. She looked for Christ *faithfully*: she stood *at the tomb*. Some find it hard to stand by a living Savior, but she stood by a dead one. Let’s look for Christ in this way, clinging to the least thing that has to do with him, staying faithful though everyone else abandons him.

Notice further that she looked for Jesus *earnestly*: she stood “*weeping*.” Those tears were like spells that held the Savior captive and made him come out and show himself to her. If you want Jesus’ presence, weep for it! If you can’t be happy unless he comes and says to you, “You are my beloved,” you will soon hear his voice. Lastly, she looked for the Savior *alone*. What did she care for angels? She turned away from them; she was searching only for her Lord. If Christ is your one and only love, if your heart has thrown out every rival, you won’t go long without the comfort of his presence. Mary Magdalene looked for him like this *because she loved much*. Let’s rouse ourselves to the same intensity of love. Let our hearts, like Mary’s, be full of Christ, and our love, like hers, will be satisfied with nothing less than himself. O Lord, show yourself to us this evening!

modern: Keep the altar of *private prayer* burning. This is the very life of all godliness. The altars of church and family borrow their fire from here, so let this one burn well. Private devotion is the very essence, the evidence and the barometer of living, heartfelt religion.

Burn the fat of your sacrifices here. Let your times of prayer alone be regular, frequent and undisturbed, if you possibly can. Earnest prayer accomplishes much. Have you nothing to pray for? Let us suggest the church, the ministry, your own soul, your children, your relatives, your neighbors, your country and the cause of God and truth throughout the world. Let’s examine ourselves on this important matter. Are we lukewarm in our private devotions? Is the fire of devotion burning dimly in our hearts? Do the chariot wheels drag heavily? If so, let’s be alarmed at this sign of decay. Let’s go with weeping and ask for the Spirit of grace and of prayer. Let’s set apart special times for extraordinary prayer. For if this fire should be smothered under the ashes of fitting in with the world, it will dim the fire on the family altar and lessen our influence in the church and in the world.

The text also applies to *the altar of the heart*. This is a golden altar indeed. God loves to see his people’s hearts glowing toward him. Let’s give God our hearts, all ablaze with love, and seek his grace so that the fire may never be put out; for it won’t burn unless the Lord keeps it burning. Many enemies will try to put it out; but if the unseen hand behind the wall pours the sacred oil on it, it will blaze higher and higher. Let’s use texts of Scripture as fuel for our heart’s fire; they are live coals. Let’s go to hear sermons; but above all, let’s spend much time alone with Jesus.

Jesus “appeared first to Mary Magdalene,” probably not only because of her great love and persistent seeking, but because, as the context hints, *she had been a special trophy of Christ’s power to set free*. Learn from this that the greatness of our sin before conversion shouldn’t make us imagine we can’t be specially favored with the very highest level of fellowship. She was someone who had left everything to become *a constant follower of the Savior*. He was her first, her chief object. Many who were on Christ’s side didn’t take up Christ’s cross; *she* did. *She spent her own money supplying his needs*. If we want to see much of Christ, let’s *serve* him. Tell me who they are who sit most often under the banner of his love and drink the deepest drafts from the cup of fellowship, and I am sure they will be those who give most, who serve best and who stay closest to the bleeding heart of their dear Lord.

But notice *how* Christ revealed himself to this grieving woman: by a *word*, “Mary.” It took only one word *in his voice*, and at once she knew him, and *her heart declared its loyalty in another word*; her heart was too full to say more. That one word would naturally be the most fitting for the occasion. It implies obedience. She said, “*Master*.” There is no state of mind in which this confession of loyalty will be too cold. No, when your spirit glows most with the heavenly fire, then you will say, “I am thy servant, thou hast loosed my bonds.” If you can say, “Master,” if you feel that his will is your will, then you stand in a happy, holy place. He must have said, “Mary,” or you couldn’t have said, “Rabboni.” See, then, from all this, how Christ honors those who honor him, how love draws our Beloved, how it takes only one word of his to turn our weeping into rejoicing, and how his presence is the heart’s sunshine.

*Work to keep a sense of your complete dependence on the Lord’s good will and pleasure for the continuance of your richest joys*. Never try to live on yesterday’s manna, and don’t look for help in Egypt. Everything must come from Jesus, or you are ruined forever. Old anointings won’t be enough to give your spirit fresh power; your head must have fresh oil poured on it from the golden horn of the sanctuary, or it will lose its glory. Today you may be on the summit of the mount of God, but he who put you there must keep you there, or you will sink far faster than you imagine. Your mountain stands firm only when he settles it in its place; if he hides his face, you will soon be troubled. If the Savior saw fit, there isn’t a window through which you see the light of heaven that he couldn’t darken in an instant. Joshua told the sun to stand still, but Jesus can wrap it in total darkness. He can take away the joy of your heart, the light of your eyes and the strength of your life. Your comforts lie in his hand, and at his will they can leave you.

Our Lord is determined that we will feel and recognize this hourly dependence, for he lets us pray only for “daily bread,” and promises only that “as our days our strength shall be.” Isn’t it best for us that it should be so, so that we may often go to his throne and be constantly reminded of his love? Oh, how rich is the grace that supplies us so continually and doesn’t hold back because of our ingratitude! The golden shower never stops; the cloud of blessing hangs over our home forever. O Lord Jesus, we bow at your feet, aware that we can do nothing at all without you; and in every favor we are privileged to receive, we adore your blessed name and acknowledge your unexhausted love.

modern:
A selfish man in trouble is extremely hard to comfort, because the springs of his comfort lie entirely within himself, and when he is sad, all his springs are dry. But a large-hearted man, full of Christian love for others, has other springs besides those within him from which to draw comfort. He can go to his God first of all and find abundant help there; and he can find reasons for comfort in things to do with the world at large, his country and, above all, the church. David was extremely sorrowful in this psalm. He wrote, “I am like an owl of the desert. I watch, and am as a sparrow alone upon the house top.” The only way he could comfort himself was with the thought that God would arise and have mercy on Zion: though *he* was sad, Zion would prosper; however low his own condition, Zion would rise.

Christian, learn to comfort yourself in God’s gracious dealings with the church. What is so dear to your Master, shouldn’t it be dearer than anything else to you? What if your own way is dark? Can’t you gladden your heart with the triumphs of his cross and the spread of his truth? Our own personal troubles are forgotten while we look not only at what God *has* done and is doing for Zion, but at the glorious things he *will yet do* for his church. Try this prescription, believer, whenever you are sad at heart and heavy in spirit: forget yourself and your little concerns, and seek the welfare and prosperity of Zion. When you kneel to pray to God, don’t limit your requests to the narrow circle of your own life, hard as it may be, but send out your longing prayers for the church’s prosperity. “Pray for the peace of Jerusalem,” and your own soul will be refreshed.

modern: Many people want to know whether they are chosen before they look to Christ, but they can’t learn it that way; it can only be discovered by “looking unto Jesus.” If you want to make sure of your own election, this is how you can assure your heart before God. Do you feel that you are a lost, guilty sinner? Go straight to the cross of Christ and tell Jesus so; and tell him that you have read in the Bible, “Him that cometh unto me, I will in no wise cast out.” Tell him that he has said, “This is a faithful saying, and worthy of all acceptation, that Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners.” Look to Jesus and believe in him, and you will have proof of your election at once, for as surely as you believe, you are chosen. If you will give yourself wholly to Christ and trust him, then you are one of God’s chosen ones; but if you stop and say, “I want to know first whether I am elect,” you don’t know what you are asking. Go to Jesus, however guilty you are, just as you are. Leave all prying questions about election alone. Go straight to Christ and hide in his wounds, and you will know your election. The assurance of the Holy Spirit will be given to you, so that you will be able to say, “I know whom I have believed, and I am persuaded that he is able to keep that which I have committed to him.” Christ was at the everlasting council; he can tell you whether you were chosen or not; but you can’t find it out any other way. Go and put your trust in him, and his answer will be, “I have loved thee with an everlasting love, therefore with lovingkindness have I drawn thee.” There will be no doubt that he has chosen *you* once you have chosen *him*.

modern:
When the prophet Elijah had received the answer to his prayer, and the fire from heaven had burned up the sacrifice in front of all the people, he called on the gathered Israelites to seize the priests of Baal, and sternly cried, “Let not one of them escape.” He took them all down to the brook Kishon and killed them there. So it must be with our sins: they are all condemned, and not one is to be spared. Our favorite sin must die. Don’t spare it for all its crying. Strike, even if it is as dear as an Isaac. Strike, for God struck at sin when it was laid on his own Son. With stern, unflinching purpose you must condemn to death the sin that was once the idol of your heart.

Do you ask how you are to do this? Jesus will be your power. You have been given grace to overcome sin in the covenant of grace; you have strength to win the victory in the crusade against the lusts within, because Christ Jesus has promised to be with you even to the end. If you want to triumph over darkness, put yourself in the presence of the Sun of Righteousness. There is no place so well suited for discovering sin, and recovering from its power and guilt, as the immediate presence of God. Job never knew how to get rid of sin half so well as when his eye of faith rested on God; then he loathed himself and repented in dust and ashes. The fine gold of the Christian is often growing dim. We need the sacred fire to burn away the dross. Let’s run to our God; he is a consuming fire. He won’t consume our spirit, but our sins. Let the goodness of God stir us to a holy jealousy and a holy vengeance against the sins that are hateful in his sight. Go out to battle with Amalek in his strength, and utterly destroy the accursed crew: let not one of them escape.

modern: The camp of Dan brought up the rear when the armies of Israel were on the march. The Danites had *the last place*; but what did the position matter, since they were as truly part of the army as the leading tribes? They followed the same pillar of cloud and fire, ate the same manna, drank from the same spiritual rock and traveled to the same inheritance. Come, my heart, cheer up, though you are last and least; it is your privilege to be in the army and to fare as well as those who lead the way. Someone must be last in honor and esteem; someone must do the humble work for Jesus; and why shouldn’t it be me? In a poor village, among ignorant country people, or in a back street among degraded sinners, I will work on and “go hindmost with my standard.”

The Danites had *a very useful place*. Stragglers have to be picked up on the march, and lost property has to be gathered from the field. Fiery spirits may dash ahead on untrodden paths to learn fresh truth and win more souls to Jesus; but some of a more conservative spirit may be well employed in reminding the church of her ancient faith and restoring her fainting sons. Every position has its duties, and God’s slow-moving children will find that their particular place is one where they can be a special blessing to the whole army.

The rear guard is *a place of danger*. There are enemies behind us as well as in front of us. Attacks may come from any side. We read that Amalek fell on Israel and killed some of the stragglers at the rear. The experienced Christian will find plenty of work for his weapons in helping those poor doubting, despondent, wavering souls who are last in faith, knowledge and joy. They mustn’t be left without help, so let it be the business of well-taught saints to carry their standards among the hindmost. My soul, watch tenderly today to help those at the back.

modern:
Locusts always keep their ranks, and although their number is legion, they don’t crowd each other so as to throw their columns into confusion. This remarkable fact of nature shows how thoroughly the Lord has filled his universe with the spirit of order, since the smallest living creatures are as much ruled by it as the rolling planets or the angelic messengers. Believers would be wise to be ruled by the same influence in all their spiritual life.

*In their Christian graces*, no one virtue should take over another’s place or eat away the life of the rest to feed itself. Love mustn’t smother honesty; courage mustn’t push weakness off the field; modesty mustn’t jostle energy; and patience mustn’t slaughter determination. So also with *our duties*: one mustn’t interfere with another. Public usefulness mustn’t harm private godliness; church work mustn’t push family worship into a corner. It is a poor thing to offer God one duty stained with the blood of another. Each thing is beautiful in its season, but not otherwise. It was to the Pharisees that Jesus said, “This ought ye to have done, and not to have left the other undone.”

The same rule applies to *our personal position*. We must take care to know our place, take it and keep to it. We must serve as the Spirit has given us ability, and not trespass on our fellow servant’s ground. Our Lord Jesus taught us not to covet the high places, but to be willing to be the least among the brothers. Far from us be an envious, ambitious spirit! Let’s feel the force of the Master’s command, and do as he tells us, keeping rank with the rest of the army. Tonight let’s see whether we are keeping the unity of the Spirit in the bonds of peace, and let our prayer be that peace and order may prevail in all the churches of the Lord Jesus.

modern:
God’s great purpose in all his works is to display his own glory. Any lower aim would be unworthy of him. But how can God’s glory be shown to fallen creatures like us? Man’s eye isn’t single. He always has a sideways glance at his own honor and too high an opinion of his own powers, and so he isn’t fit to see the glory of the Lord. Clearly, then, self must stand out of the way, so that there may be room for God to be exalted; and this is why he often brings his people into tight places and difficulties, so that, once they are aware of their own foolishness and weakness, they may be ready to see God’s majesty when he comes out to rescue them. Whoever’s life is one even, smooth path will see very little of the glory of the Lord, for he has few occasions to be emptied of himself, and so little fitness to be filled with the revelation of God. Those who sail little streams and shallow creeks know very little of the God of storms; but those who “do business in great waters,” they see his “wonders in the deep.” Among the huge Atlantic waves of bereavement, poverty, temptation and disgrace, we learn the power of Jehovah, because we feel the littleness of man.

Thank God, then, if you have been led by a rough road; it is what has given you your experience of God’s greatness and loving kindness. Your troubles have enriched you with a wealth of knowledge you could gain no other way; your trials have been the cleft in the rock where Jehovah set you, as he did his servant Moses, so that you might see his glory as it passed by. Praise God that you haven’t been left in the darkness and ignorance that constant prosperity might have brought, but that in the great fight of affliction you have been made able to see the shining out of his glory in his wonderful dealings with you.

modern:
What is weaker than the bruised reed or the smoking flax? *A reed* that grows in the fen or marsh: let the wild duck just land on it, and it snaps; let a man’s foot just brush against it, and it is bruised and broken; every wind that blows across the river sways it back and forth. You can’t imagine anything more frail or brittle, or whose life is in more danger, than a bruised reed. Then look at the smoking flax. What is it? It has a spark in it, it’s true, but it is nearly smothered; a baby’s breath might blow it out. Nothing has a more uncertain existence than its flame. *Weak things* are described here, yet Jesus says of them, “The smoking flax I will not quench; the bruised reed I will not break.”

Some of God’s children are made strong to do mighty works for him. God has his Samsons here and there, who can pull up the gates of Gaza and carry them to the top of the hill; he has a few mighty men who are lion-like, but most of his people are a timid, trembling race. They are like starlings, frightened at every passer-by: a little, fearful flock. If temptation comes, they are caught like birds in a trap; if trial threatens, they are ready to faint. Their frail little boat is tossed up and down by every wave; they are carried along like a seabird on the crest of the waves: weak things, without strength, without wisdom, without foresight. Yet weak as they are, and *because* they are so weak, this promise is made especially to them.

Here is grace and graciousness! Here is love and loving kindness! How it opens up to us the compassion of Jesus, so gentle, tender and considerate! We need never shrink from *his* touch. We need never fear a harsh word from *him*; though he might well scold us for our weakness, he doesn’t rebuke. Bruised reeds will get no blows from him, and the smoking flax no dampening frowns.

modern:
Oh, what light, what joys, what comfort, what delight of heart that man knows who has learned to feed on Jesus, and on Jesus alone! Yet our grasp of how precious Christ is remains imperfect, at best, in this life. As an old writer says, “’Tis but a taste!” We have tasted “that the Lord is gracious,” but we don’t yet know *how* good and gracious he is, although what we know of his sweetness makes us long for more. We have enjoyed the firstfruits of the Spirit, and they have set us hungering and thirsting for the fullness of the heavenly vintage. We groan within ourselves, waiting for the adoption. *Here* we are like Israel in the wilderness, who had only one cluster from Eshcol; *there* we will be in the vineyard. Here we see the manna falling small, like coriander seed; but there we will eat the bread of heaven and the old grain of the kingdom.

We are only beginners now in our spiritual education. Although we have learned the first letters of the alphabet, we can’t read words yet, much less put sentences together; but as someone says, “He that has been in heaven but five minutes, knows more than the general assembly of divines on earth.” We have many unsatisfied desires now, but soon every wish will be satisfied, and all our powers will find the sweetest work in that eternal world of joy. Christian, look ahead and taste heaven a few years early. In a very little while you will be rid of all your trials and troubles. Your eyes, now full of tears, will weep no more. You will gaze in rapture beyond words on the splendor of him who sits on the throne. Yes, more: you will sit on his throne. You will share the triumph of his glory; his crown, his joy, his paradise will be yours, and you will be joint heir with him who is the heir of all things.

modern:
By many miracles, by all kinds of mercies, by strange deliverances, Jehovah had proved himself worthy of Israel’s trust. Yet they broke down the hedges with which God had enclosed them as a sacred garden; they abandoned their own true and living God and followed false gods. The Lord constantly rebuked them for this infatuation, and our text is one example of God pleading with them: “What hast thou to do in the way of Egypt, to drink the waters of the muddy river?” for that is how it may be translated. “Why do you wander so far, and leave your own cool stream from Lebanon? Why do you abandon Jerusalem to turn aside to Noph and Tahapanes? Why are you so strangely set on mischief that you can’t be content with what is good and wholesome, but must go after what is evil and deceitful?”

Isn’t there a word of pleading and warning here for the Christian? True believer, called by grace and washed in the precious blood of Jesus, you have tasted better drink than the muddy river of this world’s pleasures can give you. You have had fellowship with Christ; you have known the joy of seeing Jesus and leaning your head on his breast. Do the trifles, the songs, the honors and the merriment of this earth satisfy you after that? Have you eaten the bread of angels, and can you live on pig food? Good Rutherford once said, “I have tasted of Christ’s own manna, and it hath put my mouth out of taste for the brown bread of this world’s joys.” I think it should be the same with you. If you are wandering after the waters of Egypt, oh, come back quickly to the one living fountain. The waters of Sihor may be sweet to the Egyptians, but they will prove only bitterness to you. What have you to do with them? *Jesus asks you this question this evening*: what will you answer him?

modern: Reassured by the word of the Lord, the poor, trembling citizens of Zion grew bold and shook their heads at Sennacherib’s boastful threats. Strong faith enables God’s servants to look with calm contempt on their haughtiest enemies. *We know that our enemies are attempting the impossible*. They are trying to destroy the eternal life, which can’t die while Jesus lives; to overthrow the citadel, against which the gates of hell will not prevail. They kick against the goads, to their own wounding, and charge the bosses of Jehovah’s shield, to their own hurt.

*We know their weakness*. What are they but men? And what is man but a worm? They roar and swell like the waves of the sea, foaming out their own shame. When the Lord arises, they will fly like chaff before the wind and be burned up like crackling thorns. Their utter powerlessness to harm the cause of God and his truth may make the weakest soldiers in Zion’s ranks laugh them to scorn.

Above all, *we know that the Most High is with us*, and when he puts on his armor, where are his enemies? If he comes out from his place, the broken pots of the earth won’t fight their Maker for long. His rod of iron will smash them in pieces like a potter’s jar, and their very memory will perish from the earth. Away, then, with all fears; the kingdom is safe in the King’s hands. Let’s shout for joy, for the Lord reigns, and his enemies will be like straw for the dunghill.

modern:
Can you answer this, believer? Can you find any reason why you are so often mourning instead of rejoicing? Why give in to gloomy forebodings? Who told you that the night would never end in day? Who told you that the sea of circumstances would ebb out until nothing was left but miles and miles of the mud of dreadful poverty? Who told you that the winter of your discontent would go on from frost to frost, from snow and ice and hail to deeper snow and a still heavier storm of despair? Don’t you know that day follows night, that flood comes after ebb, that spring and summer come after winter? Hope, then! Hope always! For God doesn’t fail you. Don’t you know that your God loves you in the middle of all this? Mountains hidden in darkness are as real as in daylight, and God’s love is as true to you now as it was in your brightest moments. No father disciplines all the time. Your Lord hates the rod as much as you do; he only cares to use it for the very reason that should make you willing to accept it: that it works for your lasting good.

You will yet climb Jacob’s ladder with the angels and see the one who sits at the top of it, your covenant God. You will yet, among the splendors of eternity, forget the trials of time, or remember them only to bless the God who led you through them and worked your lasting good by them. Come, sing in the middle of tribulation. Rejoice even as you pass through the furnace. Make the wilderness blossom like the rose! Make the desert ring with your exultant joy, for these light afflictions will soon be over, and then, “for ever with the Lord,” your happiness will never fade.

modern:
Christ Jesus is joined to his people in the union of marriage. In love he betrothed his church as a pure virgin, long before she fell under the yoke of slavery. Full of burning love, he labored, like Jacob for Rachel, until her whole bride-price had been paid; and now, having sought her by his Spirit and brought her to know and love him, he is waiting for the glorious hour when their shared happiness will be crowned at the wedding supper of the Lamb. The glorious Bridegroom hasn’t yet presented his betrothed, perfected and complete, before the Majesty of heaven; she hasn’t yet actually entered into the enjoyment of her honors as his wife and queen. She is still a wanderer in a world of sorrow, a dweller in the tents of Kedar. But she is even now the bride, the wife of Jesus, dear to his heart, precious in his sight, written on his hands and united with his person.

On earth he carries out toward her all the loving duties of a husband. He makes rich provision for her needs, pays all her debts, lets her take his name and share in all his wealth. And he will never act any other way toward her. He will never mention the word divorce, for “He hateth putting away.” Death must break the marriage tie between the most loving of mortals, but it can’t break the links of this immortal marriage. In heaven they don’t marry, but are like the angels of God; yet there is this one marvelous exception to the rule, for in heaven Christ and his church will celebrate their joyful wedding. This union, as it is more lasting, so it is closer than earthly marriage. However pure and fervent a husband’s love may be, it is only a faint picture of the flame that burns in the heart of Jesus. Beyond every human union is that mystical clinging to the church for which Christ left his Father and became one flesh with her.

modern:
If there is one place where our Lord Jesus most fully becomes the joy and comfort of his people, it is where he plunged deepest into the depths of sorrow. Come here, gracious souls, and see the man in the garden of Gethsemane: see his heart so brimming with love that he can’t hold it in, so full of sorrow that it must find an outlet. See the bloody sweat as it oozes from every pore of his body and falls on the ground. See the man as they drive the nails into his hands and feet. Look up, repenting sinners, and see the sorrowful image of your suffering Lord. Look at him as the ruby drops stand on the crown of thorns and adorn with priceless gems the crown of the King of Misery. See the man when all his bones are out of joint, and he is poured out like water and brought into the dust of death; God has forsaken him, and hell surrounds him. Look and see: was there ever any sorrow like his sorrow, which is done to him? All you who pass by, come near and look at this spectacle of grief: unique, unparalleled, a wonder to men and angels, a marvel without match. See the Emperor of Sorrow, who had no equal or rival in his agonies! Gaze at him, you mourners, for if there isn’t comfort in a crucified Christ, there is no joy on earth or in heaven. If there isn’t hope in the ransom price of his blood, then, you harps of heaven, there is no joy in you, and the right hand of God will know no pleasures forevermore.

We have only to sit more constantly at the foot of the cross to be less troubled by our doubts and sorrows. We have only to see *his* sorrows, and we will be ashamed to mention *ours*. We have only to gaze into his wounds to heal our own. If we want to live rightly, it must be by thinking on his death; if we want to rise to dignity, it must be by considering his humiliation and his sorrow.

modern: Edom owed Israel brotherly kindness in her time of need, but instead the men of Esau made common cause with Israel’s enemies. Special stress in this sentence falls on the word *thou*, as when Caesar cried to Brutus, “and *thou* Brutus.” A bad action can be all the worse because of who did it. When *we* sin, who are heaven’s chosen favorites, we sin with emphasis. Ours is a crying offense, because we are so specially favored. If an angel were to lay his hand on us when we are doing wrong, he would need no other rebuke than the question, “What, *you*? What are *you* doing here?” Much forgiven, much rescued, much taught, much enriched, much blessed, will we dare to put out our hand to evil? God forbid!

A few minutes of confession may do you good this morning, dear reader. Have you never been like the wicked? At an evening party certain men laughed at dirty talk, and the joke wasn’t altogether offensive to your ear; *even you were like one of them*. When hard things were said about the ways of God, you kept shyly silent; and so, to onlookers, *you were like one of them*. When worldly people were bargaining in the market and driving hard bargains, weren’t you like one of them? When they were chasing empty things with a hunter’s stride, weren’t you as greedy for gain as they were? Could anyone see any difference between you and them? *Is there any difference*? Here we come to close quarters. Be honest with your own soul, and make sure you are a new creation in Christ Jesus; but once that is sure, walk watchfully, so that no one can ever again say, “Even thou wast as one of them.” You wouldn’t want to share their eternal doom, so why be like them here? Don’t come into their secret, or you will come into their ruin. Side with God’s afflicted people, and not with the world.

modern:
“Cleanseth,” says the text, not “*shall* cleanse.” Multitudes think that as a dying hope they may look forward to pardon. Oh, how infinitely better to have cleansing now than to depend on the bare possibility of forgiveness when I come to die! Some imagine that a sense of pardon can only be reached after many years of Christian experience. But forgiveness of sin is a *present* thing: a privilege for today, a joy for this very hour. The moment a sinner trusts Jesus, he is fully forgiven.

The text, being in the present tense, also shows *continuance*. It was “cleanseth” yesterday, it is “cleanseth” today, it will be “cleanseth” tomorrow. It will always be so for you, Christian, until you cross the river; every hour you may come to this fountain, for it cleanses still. Notice too the *completeness* of the cleansing: “The blood of Jesus Christ his Son cleanseth us from *all* sin”; not only from sin, but “from all sin.” Reader, I can’t tell you how very sweet this word is, but I pray God the Holy Spirit to give you a taste of it. Our sins against God are many and of every kind. But whether the bill is small or large, the same receipt can settle the one as well as the other. The blood of Jesus Christ is as blessed and divine a payment for the sins of cursing Peter as for the shortcomings of loving John. Our sin is gone, all gone at once, and all gone forever. Blessed completeness! What a sweet subject to dwell on as you give yourself to sleep.
